overview.heading: Torpedo boat Drazki
overview.text: Drazki (Дръзки, “Daring”) is a small, fast warship built in France for the Bulgarian Navy. She is 38 metres long, reached 26 knots and carried torpedoes as her main weapon. On the night of 21 November 1912 she crept up to the Ottoman cruiser Hamidiye and hit it with a torpedo – the most famous moment in the history of the Bulgarian Navy. Today she stands in the Sea Garden in Varna as a museum ship.
overview.fact: In Bulgarian a torpedo boat is a “миноносец” – a “mine carrier”. When torpedoes were new they were called “self-propelled mines”, and the name stayed.
overview.hint: Click any part of the ship or pick one from the list. Drag to look around, scroll or pinch to zoom. Set the speed, turn the torpedo tubes and fire, or open the cutaway to look inside.

controls.fireTitle: Turn the twin tube at least 30°, then fire. The two tubes take turns: one fires to the right, the other to the left.
controls.cutawayTitle: Take away the starboard side plating to look inside

hull.name: Hull
hull.text: The steel body of the ship: long, narrow and light, so she could slip through the water fast. Drazki is almost nine times longer than she is wide. Below the waterline the hull is painted red, a white stripe marks the waterline, and the sides above are grey, which makes a warship harder to see at sea.

forecastle.name: Forecastle
forecastle.text: The raised, rounded deck at the front. Its curved “turtle-back” shape lets the waves that break over the bow run off quickly to the sides. Under it live the crew, and the bow torpedo tube runs through it.

deck.name: Main deck
deck.text: The working deck in the middle and at the stern, painted red-brown. The funnel casings, the ventilator, the twin torpedo tube and the aft steering wheel stand on it. The raised casings round the funnels cover the boiler rooms below; between them a hatch leads down to the stokehold.

stem.name: Stem
stem.text: The front edge of the hull. Drazki has a straight, almost vertical stem that cuts through the waves. At its top you can see the round cap of the bow torpedo tube.

breakwater.name: Breakwater
breakwater.text: A breakwater split in two: at the front of each bridge wing a curved plate, shaped like a snow plough, curves from the outer corner in and forward to a point at the alley, hollow towards the bow, its top leaning forward. Behind it the side under the wing is open. When a wave comes over the bow, the plates throw the water aside before it reaches the bridge and the conning tower.

bulkheads.name: Watertight bulkheads
bulkheads.text: Steel walls across the hull that divide it into separate rooms. If the hull is holed, water fills only one room and the others keep the ship afloat. Turn on the cutaway to see them.

portholes.name: Portholes
portholes.text: Small round windows with thick glass and brass rims. They let daylight into the crew's quarters in the bow and the officers' cabin at the stern. In bad weather a steel cover was screwed down over the glass.

nameplate.name: Name plate
nameplate.text: A brass oval with the ship's name, ДРЪЗКИ, on both sides of the bow. Drazki means “daring” or “bold”. Her five sisters had names of the same kind: Smeli (Brave), Hrabri (Valiant), Strogi (Stern), Letyashti (Flying) and Shumni (Noisy).

boilers.name: Boilers
boilers.text: Two water-tube boilers make the steam. A coal fire burns at the bottom, and water runs through hundreds of thin tubes above it, so it heats up very quickly. The steam collects in the big drum on top and goes to the engine. Stokers shovelled coal into the fire doors all the time.
boilers.fact: The stokehold between the two boilers was the hottest place on the ship. The big ventilator pushed air down to the fires so the coal burned faster.

coalBunkers.name: Coal bunkers
coalBunkers.text: Store rooms for coal along both sides of the boiler rooms. When full they held about 11 tonnes – enough to steam about 500 nautical miles at a steady 16 knots, much less at full speed.

engine.name: Steam engine
engine.text: A vertical triple-expansion engine. Steam pushes a piston in a small cylinder, then in a middle one, then in a big one, so it works three times before it is used up. The pistons turn the crankshaft, and the crankshaft turns the propeller. Set a speed and turn on the cutaway to watch it run.

condenser.name: Condenser
condenser.text: Sea water is salty and would ruin the boilers, so the used steam is not thrown away. In the condenser it flows over pipes cooled by sea water, turns back into fresh water and is pumped back to the boilers.

shaft.name: Propeller shaft
shaft.text: A long steel rod that carries the turning force of the engine through the bottom of the hull to the propeller. Where it leaves the hull, a stern tube keeps the sea out; near the propeller, a bracket holds it steady.

propeller.name: Propeller
propeller.text: Three bronze blades shaped like part of a screw. As the propeller turns, it pushes water backwards and the ship moves forwards. At full speed it turned several times every second.

rudder.name: Rudder
rudder.text: The flat blade behind the propeller that steers the ship. When the helmsman turns the wheel, chains move the rudder to one side, the water presses against it and the stern swings round. On Drazki the rudder hangs right at the end of the stern, as on many French torpedo boats of the time. It hangs on a stock just aft of the hull; its top rises in a curved shoulder to the stock, which runs up to deck height, where a tiller leads forward over the deck. A guard bar runs from the keel down under the propeller to the foot of the rudder, so the blades cannot strike anything. All of it is painted red.

funnels.name: Funnels
funnels.text: Two tall chimneys carry the smoke and hot gases from the boilers up and away from the deck. Their height also helps the fires to draw air. A good stoker kept the smoke thin: thick black smoke could be seen from far away and give the boat away.

shellHole.name: Shell hole
shellHole.text: During the night attack on 21 November 1912 a fragment of an enemy shell went through the second funnel. The hole was never repaired. The funnel is on the museum ship in Varna today, and the hole is kept in memory of the Bulgarian Navy's first victory.

ventilators.name: Ventilator
ventilators.text: One big round pipe stands beside the stokehold hatch. At the top it bends over, and its mouth, with a rolled rim, is turned inboard. It catches the wind and sends fresh air down to the boiler fires, which needed a lot of air to burn hot. Inside it is painted red.

skylight.name: Engine-room skylight
skylight.text: A low casing over the engine room, joined to the aft funnel casing a step lower. Three flat hatches, each as wide as the skylight, have round deck lights along their edges. They let daylight in and heat out, and open wide for work on the engine. Forward of them a small hatch with three deck lights and a V-shaped handle leads down; a second one like it is on the deck, under the twin tube.

twinTubes.name: Twin torpedo tube
twinTubes.text: The main weapon: two 450 mm tubes side by side on a turntable, facing opposite ways. When the crew turned the turntable, one tube pointed to the right side of the ship and the other to the left, so they could fire at a target on either side. A small charge of gunpowder pushed the torpedo out over the side, and the curved “spoon” at the muzzle guided it as it left. Turn the tubes and press Fire!

bowTube.name: Bow torpedo tube
bowTube.text: A third tube is built into the bow and points straight ahead. To use it, the whole ship had to be aimed at the target. Its round cap shows on the stem; inside, the tube runs through the crew's quarters.

torpedo.name: Torpedo
torpedo.text: A torpedo is a small underwater craft with its own engine. Compressed air drives two propellers that turn in opposite directions, so it does not roll. A gyroscope keeps it on course, and the explosive charge is in the bronze head. Drazki carried spare torpedoes on deck to reload the tubes.

torpedoDavit.name: Torpedo davit
torpedoDavit.text: A small crane at the side of the deck. With it the crew lifted torpedoes on board from a boat or the pier, and swung them across to the tubes.

foreGun.name: 47 mm guns
foreGun.text: Two quick-firing Hotchkiss guns, one on each side, opposite each other between the forward funnel and the conning tower. Each stands half on the deck edge and half on a long, narrow platform of perforated steel that sticks out from the hull side, with a rail round it, so it can fire forward, abeam and aft. The gunner aimed it with a shoulder piece, moving the whole gun with his body. The guns were meant for small enemy boats; the torpedoes were the real weapon. The builder's description of 1908, navypedia and the 2025 reconstruction show two guns; the museum ship today has one.

magazine.name: Magazine
magazine.text: A locked room deep in the hull where the ammunition was kept, below the waterline and away from the fires. In October 1942 an explosion in a magazine sank Drazki in Varna harbour. She was raised, repaired and sailed again.

conningTower.name: Conning tower
conningTower.text: The command post at the front of the ship. Its steel walls protect the commander and the helmsman, who look out through three fan-shaped windows with wipers; in battle, hinged armour flaps inside close them. The main wheel, the compass and the telegraph are here. From here the commander gave the orders for steering, speed and firing.

wheel.name: Steering wheel
wheel.text: The main wheel is fixed to the front wall of the conning tower. Its shaft goes through the wall to the steering gear under the hood, and from there chains and rods run along the deck to the rudder at the stern.

aftWheel.name: Aft steering wheel
aftWheel.text: A second wheel on the stern deck. Its barrel winds two chains: rollers lead them out to the sides, they run aft along the rails, and rollers at the stern turn them in to the end of the rudder's tiller: turn the wheel and the rudder turns. So the boat could still be steered if the gear forward was damaged. Just forward of the wheel stands a pedestal with a flat round top. Aft of the wheel, on the port side, stands a tall cage of bent tube over a low horseshoe-shaped steel wall with a shallow dish inside; it is open at the back. The use of both is not known – one of them may have carried a compass for the aft helmsman.

bridge.name: Bridge wings
bridge.text: Two platforms of perforated steel plate, one on each side of the conning tower and the forecastle, level with the top of the forecastle. Their outer edge stands out over the hull side, carried by five perforated rib brackets. Between them the plain forecastle deck forms an alley, where the hand winch stands. Water runs straight through the holes.

compass.name: Compass
compass.text: The magnetic compass in its binnacle stands on the floor of the conning tower, just aft of the wheel, under the helmsman's eyes. A steel ship disturbs a compass, so the two iron balls and the brass bars beside it correct the error.

telegraph.name: Engine telegraph
telegraph.text: It stands inside the conning tower, beside the wheel. There were no telephones on board. To change speed, the officer moves this handle to an order such as “Half ahead”. A bell rings in the engine room, a matching dial shows the order, and the engineers set the engine. Move the speed slider and watch the handle.

mast.name: Mast
mast.text: The mast carries the signal yard, the masthead light and a high place for the lookout. Flags hoisted on the yard were how ships talked to each other in daylight.

navLights.name: Navigation lights
navLights.text: Red on the left (port) side, green on the right (starboard) side and white on the mast. At night other ships can tell which way you are heading from the colours they see. In a night attack, of course, every light was switched off.

ensign.name: Naval ensign
ensign.text: The flag of the Bulgarian Navy from 1879 to 1944: white, green and red stripes, with a red square at the staff showing a golden crowned lion. It flies from a staff at the very end of the stern, on top of a horseshoe-shaped arch of tube in the stern rail; the rudder head swings freely under the arch.

anchors.name: Anchors
anchors.text: Two anchors lie on the forecastle, ready to drop. Their heavy chains run to the windlass. On the seabed an anchor digs in with its pointed flukes and holds the ship in place.

windlass.name: Windlass
windlass.text: A winch for the anchor chains. Its notched wheels grip the links; sailors turned the handles to haul the anchor up.

bowSpar.name: Bow spar
bowSpar.text: A short pole sticks out over the bow torpedo tube, with a ball of chain at its end. It was probably a fender that kept the bow off a pier or another ship; the sources do not say.

winch.name: Hand winch
winch.text: On the forecastle in front of the conning tower, between the bridge wings. Two sailors turn the cranks; through the gears the two waisted drums turn slowly but with great force and haul in the mooring ropes.

bollards.name: Bollards
bollards.text: Pairs of short steel posts on deck. Mooring ropes are wound round them in figures of eight to tie the ship to a pier or to another ship.

rails.name: Rails and nets
rails.text: Iron posts bolted to the hull side carry two thick ropes along both sides of the deck. Along the middle of the ship a net like a fishing net hangs from the top rope. On a narrow, rolling deck they stop sailors – and their gear – from going overboard.

hatches.name: Hatches
hatches.text: Openings in the deck with raised edges and tight lids. Ladders lead down through them to the crew's quarters, the officers' cabin and the engine room. In rough weather the lids were closed to keep the water out.

dinghy.name: Ship's boats
dinghy.text: Two small rowing boats, one on each side of the stern. At sea each lies on its side against the hull at rail level, bottom outward and a canvas cover over the open side, held by crossed straps. The crew used them to go ashore, to carry messages, or to pick up someone who fell overboard.

lifebuoys.name: Lifebuoys
lifebuoys.text: Red-and-white rings that float. If someone falls into the sea, a lifebuoy is thrown to them to hold on to until they are picked up.

crewQuarters.name: Crew's quarters
crewQuarters.text: The sailors lived in the bow: up to thirty men in a room smaller than a classroom. They slept in narrow bunks, ate at a small table and kept their things in lockers. The bow torpedo tube ran right through the room.
crewQuarters.fact: The poet Nikola Vaptsarov served on Drazki in 1930–1931, while he studied at the naval school in Varna.

wardroom.name: Officers' cabin
wardroom.text: At the stern is the wardroom, where the commander and his few officers ate, worked on their charts and slept on the sofas. It is quieter here than in the bow, but the propeller turns right underneath.

galley.name: Galley
galley.text: The ship's kitchen: an iron stove in a small open shelter on deck. Cooking on deck kept the heat, the smoke and the danger of fire out of the cramped hull. The stove is still on the museum ship.
